documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the field of criminal forensics in India by enhancing the efficiency, speed and accuracy of criminal investigations. AI-powered technologies such as facial recognition systems, predictive analytics, biometric identification, digital surveillance and machine learning algorithms are increasingly being used by investigative agencies to analyse evidence, identify suspects and detect criminal patterns. In the context of rising cybercrimes, organized crimes and digital offences, AI has emerged as a significant tool for modernizing forensic science and strengthening the criminal justice system. Despite its advantages, the use of AI in criminal forensics also raises several legal, ethical and constitutional concerns. Issues relating to privacy, data protection, algorithmic bias, lack of transparency and reliability of AI-generated evidence pose serious challenges to the Indian legal framework. The absence of comprehensive legislation regulating AI usage in criminal investigations further creates uncertainty regarding accountability and admissibility of AI-based evidence in courts. Additionally, overdependence on automated systems may threaten fundamental rights and procedural fairness if proper safeguards are not implemented. This paper critically examines the opportunities and challenges associated with the application of AI in modern criminal forensics in India. It explores the technological advancements, their impact on forensic investigations and the need for a balanced legal and regulatory framework that ensures both effective crime detection and protection of individual rights in a society.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This project is a scoping review entitled "Artificial Intelligence in Pharmaceutical Clinical Decision-Making." It maps the scientific evidence on artificial intelligence (AI) tools that pharmacists use to support clinical decision-making in pharmaceutical services. AI is increasingly used in healthcare for diagnosis, prognosis and clinical decision support. In pharmacy, it has potential in prescription analysis, drug interaction screening, dose adjustment and adverse event monitoring. However, its use in pharmacy practice is still incipient and mostly oriented toward operational tasks such as inventory management and process optimization. Evidence on the direct clinical use of AI by pharmacists, and on its effects on patient safety and clinical outcomes, remains scarce and dispersed. A scoping review suits this emerging, heterogeneous field, where there is not yet enough homogeneous evidence for a synthesis of effectiveness. The review is part of the project SisAPEC Farma, aims to develop AI tools to support pharmaceutical clinical decision-making. The review will therefore provide the scientific grounding for the system's pharmaceutical module. Objective The primary objective is to map the scientific evidence on the use of AI-based tools employed by pharmacists to support clinical decision-making in pharmaceutical services, in Brazil or in other countries. The research question follows the Population–Concept–Context (PCC) framework: Population: pharmacists involved in clinical services or direct patient care. Concept: the use, development, evaluation or implementation of AI-based tools or systems to support clinical decision-making. Context: clinical services provided by pharmacists in different practice settings (primary care, community pharmacies, hospitals, outpatient services and clinics). Methods The review follows the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology, which builds on the Arksey and O'Malley framework. The protocol was written using the guidance and template of Lely et al. (2023), and the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) will guide reporting. Eligibility: The review will include studies involving pharmacists working in clinical services or direct patient care. These studies must describe, develop, evaluate or implement AI tools (machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, generative AI, expert systems and AI-based clinical decision support systems) applied to clinical pharmacy practice. Studies with peripheral pharmacist involvement will be excluded, as will studies focused exclusively on non-clinical activities (administrative management, logistics, inventory, dispensing automation) and studies on industrial or drug-discovery applications with no clinical pharmacy use. Only records with available full text will be included. No language or date limits will be applied. Search strategy: The strategy was developed for MEDLINE/PubMed and adapted to Embase, the Virtual Health Library (BVS), Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL and the Cochrane Library. Grey literature (Google Scholar, ProQuest and OpenGrey), hand-searching of reference lists and expert consultation will complement it. Controlled vocabularies (MeSH, DeCS, Emtree) and free-text terms will be combined. Because Population and Context cover the same conceptual universe (pharmacists and the clinical pharmacy services in which they work), they are combined with OR, and this block is then combined with the AI concept block using AND. Selection and charting: Records will be deduplicated in EndNote 20 and screened in Rayyan by two independent, blinded reviewers in two stages (title/abstract, then full text). Disagreements will be resolved by consensus or by a third reviewer, and reasons for exclusion at full-text stage will be recorded. Data will be charted independently by two reviewers using a piloted Excel form adapted from JBI SUMARI. It will cover study identification, context and population, AI tool characteristics, results, barriers and facilitators, and gaps and opportunities. Synthesis: Analysis will be descriptive, using absolute and relative frequencies. Where pertinent, basic qualitative content analysis will combine an inductive and a deductive step. Results will be presented in tables, figures, narrative summaries and a PRISMA-ScR flow diagram. Any AI-based automation used to support the review will operate only under supervision, with all decisions validated by human reviewers. Expected Results The review is expected to produce a comprehensive map of the nature and extent of the evidence on AI tools used by pharmacists for clinical decision-making, including the types of tools, their functionalities and the clinical processes they support; a characterization of the available evidence on usability, acceptability, feasibility, performance, implementation and clinical impact, showing where evidence is concentrated and where it is lacking; an identification of the practice settings and countries in which these technologies have been most studied. A systematized overview of the technical, ethical, regulatory and organizational barriers and facilitators to implementing AI in clinical pharmacy; a clear identification of research gaps and unmet needs, pointing to opportunities for developing or improving AI solutions aligned with real clinical pharmacy needs and; by clarifying what is known and what is still missing, the review is expected to advance the field. It will support the safe, evidence-based development and implementation of AI in clinical pharmacy, including the pharmaceutical module of SisAPEC Farma. It will also inform future research, practice and policy.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This scoping review aims to systematically map and synthesize the existing literature on artificial intelligence (AI) literacy and readiness among nursing students in educational and clinical learning contexts. The review will examine how AI literacy and readiness are conceptualized, defined, and measured among nursing students. It will identify the levels and dimensions of AI-related knowledge, skills, competencies, attitudes, confidence, and preparedness reported in the literature, as well as factors associated with students' readiness to engage with AI technologies in nursing education and future professional practice. The review will also explore the educational strategies, training initiatives, assessment instruments, and institutional factors discussed in relation to the development of AI literacy and readiness among nursing students. The review will be guided by the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and structured using the Population–Concept–Context (PCC) framework. Relevant evidence from quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods studies will be considered, subject to predefined eligibility criteria. A systematic search of relevant bibliographic databases and supplementary sources will be undertaken, followed by transparent study selection, data charting, and descriptive and thematic mapping of the available evidence. Findings will be reported in accordance with the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), where applicable. The anticipated outcome is a comprehensive overview of the scope, characteristics, measurement approaches, educational applications, and research gaps relating to AI literacy and readiness among nursing students. The findings may inform future research, nursing curricula, AI-related educational interventions, and the development of relevant competencies and assessment frameworks.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: In contemporary digital society, artificial intelligence literacy (AI literacy) has become a key competence that enables citizens to understand and actively participate in increasingly automated environments. However, despite the rapid growth of scientific output, partly driven by tools such as ChatGPT, the literature reveals substantial conceptual fragmentation that hinders an integrated understanding of its educational and ethical dimensions. In this context, this study aimed to analyze the intellectual evolution and conceptual structure of research on AI literacy, based on Scopus-indexed literature. A bibliometric methodology was applied to a corpus of 2,645 documents using scientific mapping techniques to identify publication patterns, collaboration networks, and dominant thematic streams. The results reveal an accelerated expansion of the field and a shift from early approaches focused primarily on educational contexts such as K-12 education and computational thinking toward more complex frameworks that incorporate algorithmic ethics, psychological acceptance of technology, critical thinking, and academic integrity challenges associated with generative AI (GenAI). Overall, this study contributes to the educational technology literature by providing a longitudinal bibliometric interpretation of the evolution of AI literacy and by identifying emerging research agendas related to GenAI, ethical reasoning, and critical digital competencies in contemporary education.

This study aims to analyze the influence of Artificial Intelligence Marketing and Consumer Trust on Purchase Intention in Generation Z consumers. A sample of 100 Generation Z respondents who actively use digital media and are exposed to AI-based marketing was selected using purposive sampling techniques. Data were collected through a Likert scale questionnaire of 1–5 and analyzed using multiple linear regression, t-test, F test, and determination coefficient (R2) test. The results showed that partially, Artificial Intelligence Marketing (t = 12.021; p = 0.000) and Consumer Trust (t = 7.873; p = 0.000) had a positive and significant effect on Purchase Intent. Simultaneously, Artificial Intelligence Marketing and Consumer Trust had a significant effect on Purchase Intention (F = 278.811; p = 0.000). A determination coefficient value (R2) of 0.852 showed that 85.2% of the variation in Purchase Intention was influenced by these two variables, while the remaining 14.8% was influenced by other factors outside the model. This study concludes that optimizing personalization-based AI marketing strategies coupled with maintaining consumer trust is a key determinant in encouraging Generation Z's buying interest.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used across scholarly writing, peer review, and editorial workflows, creating new research integrity questions about attribution, accountability, and disclosure. We measured how explicit artificial intelligence (AI) transparency statements are appearing in published medical literature and whether scalable full-text methods can monitor their adoption across journals and specialties. We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional bibliometric analysis of 97,916 English-language medical journal articles published from 2015 through April 2026 across 14 medical and surgical fields. Full text was retrieved from PubMed Central XML or publisher-hosted article files and classified with a large language model for positive AI-use disclosure, explicit statements of non-use, named tools, use cases, and statement location. Validation used pre-ChatGPT specificity, second-model agreement in 10,979 articles, and blinded human review of 300 stratified cases by 2 independent reviewers with adjudication. All rates were recalculated excluding Frontiers journals, whose submission workflow applies a standardized AI declaration. Any AI transparency statement increased from 1.4% in 2023 to 22.4% in January-April 2026, or 9.9% excluding Frontiers journals. Positive disclosure reached 7.3% (6.2% excluding Frontiers), while negative disclosure reached 15.1% (3.7% excluding Frontiers). Frontiers contributed 6.1% of articles but 71.1% of negative disclosures. Health Informatics and Digital Medicine had the highest positive disclosure rate during 2023–2026 (11.1%; 10.5% excluding Frontiers). Among 91 journals with at least 20 classified articles in 2025–2026, statement rates ranged from 0 to 100%, and all 3 journals at 100% were Frontiers titles. Language refinement was the most common disclosed use (72.8%). Inter-model agreement was high (Cohen kappa = 0.96 positive, 0.98 negative), and blinded human review confirmed 93.3% and 97.3% of these classifications, respectively. AI transparency statements are becoming a measurable publication-governance signal, but their prevalence is driven substantially by publisher submission infrastructure rather than author initiative: one publisher accounted for 71.1% of all negative disclosures. Near-universal declaration capture is therefore achievable through workflow design, and low observed disclosure rates may reflect missing declaration fields more than author reticence. Scalable full-text monitoring may help editors, publishers, and research integrity stakeholders evaluate policy implementation and distinguish assistive from generative AI use.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Translation of the drop-in gamma probe transformed radioguided robot-assisted prostate cancer (PCa) surgery. This study evaluated whether digitization of radiometric signals could allow conversion into more easier to interpret Augmented Reality radiation mapping (AR RM ) displays. 20 PCa patients were included who underwent robot-assisted sentinel node (SN)- and prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) radioguided resections (24 SNs, 16 PSMA-avid nodes and 1 PSMA-avid primary tumor). Radiometric probe counts/s (dimensionless) synchronized with positional probe data allowed the retrospective creation of dynamic AR RM overlays in two dimensions. Artificial intelligence was used to segment out, and automatically track, surgical instruments and dynamically de-occlude the AR RM displays accordingly. Retrospective scoring by end-users indicated a 72.5% preference for the AR RM displays compared to the currently available radiometric display (bipolar scale; median ≥2; p < 0.001). Thus, indicating that video-feed embedded AR RM visualizations provide a digital means to further advance the surgeon’s perception of intraoperative molecular imaging.

Purpose This paper aims to explore the thermal energy transfer in radiative nanofluid flow of oxytactic microorganisms under zero mass flux conditions with potential application in engineering systems. The investigation concerns free convection over an isothermal perpendicular cone in a permeable medium filled with a nanofluid. Design/methodology/approach A deep learning-based nonlinear autoregressive exogenous neural network optimized with Levenberg–Marquardt backpropagation (NARX-DNN-LMBP) is designed for the model of the radiative nanofluidic flow with microorganism (RNF-MO). It includes the effects of Brownian motion, solar radiation, thermophoresis, convective heating, suspended nanoparticles and oxytactic microorganisms along with zero mass flux boundary conditions. The synthetic data set is created using the Lobatto IIIA numerical solver and then randomly split into training, validation and test sets used to develop the neural network. Findings The proposed NARX-DNN-LMBP approach is found to be effective in predicting the RNF-MO model for various physical scenarios with mean squared error as low as 10−10. It is further evaluated with the mean squared error convergence trends, error histograms and error autocorrelation analysis to show accurate and reliable computational performance. Originality/value The novelty is achieved by coupling the NARX-DNN-LMBP deep learning framework with the Lobatto IIIA solver for fluid flow of complex radiative nanofluid with oxytactic microorganisms under zero mass flux condition. By simultaneously considering Brownian motion, convective heating, solar radiation and thermophoresis, a comprehensive computational framework for advanced thermal transport analysis can be provided.

This article examines international experience with AI-based career guidance systems and assesses the conditions for introducing them in Uzbekistan’s education system. Using a qualitative comparative design, it compares the platforms of the United States, South Korea, Singapore and Germany against five criteria and rates Uzbekistan on the same basis. The results show that success depends more on data quality, links to study and job opportunities, and human counsellors than on algorithmic sophistication. The article proposes a three-stage single-platform model that turns a student’s portfolio into occupation match percentages and direct applications

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored in tissue engineering as a data-driven tool for linking biomaterial composition, scaffold architecture, fabrication parameters, and biological responses. Machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches have been applied to predict scaffold properties such as mechanical behavior, porosity, and degradation, and to support biomaterial selection and optimization of biofabrication parameters, including extrusion pressure, printing speed, and material formulation. AI-assisted imaging and sensing can also support in-line monitoring of printing quality and provide a basis for emerging feedback-enabled and adaptive biofabrication strategies. Beyond fabrication, data-driven and hybrid computational models are being investigated for analysis of cell–material interactions and tissue microenvironments, including spatial, mechanical, and transport-related phenomena. AI-assisted approaches have also been applied to nanocarrier formulation and drug-release prediction, where physicochemical and environmental variables can be integrated to support formulation design and forecast release behavior. Emerging digital-twin frameworks extend these concepts by combining patient-specific imaging, computational modeling, and AI-assisted design to support individualized scaffold development. However, most current applications remain computational, retrospective, in vitro, or preclinical, and high predictive performance does not necessarily indicate translational readiness. Limited and heterogeneous datasets, insufficient external validation, fabrication constraints, bioink rheology, crosslinking variability, cell viability, model interpretability, and regulatory requirements continue to limit reproducibility and clinical translation. This review therefore provides a pragmatic, application-oriented assessment of AI in tissue engineering, emphasizing demonstrated capabilities, current validation levels, and the remaining gap between computational prediction and reproducible, clinically relevant biofabrication.

With the continuous development of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, smart home systems have gradually evolved from traditional automated control modes toward intelligent systems with environmental perception, autonomous decision-making, and proactive service capabilities. However, existing smart homes still face problems such as a single mode of interaction, insufficient intelligent proactivity, and limited scene adaptability. Based on relevant research results in recent years, this paper systematically reviews the application progress of AI technology in the smart home field, focusing on key directions such as the Internet of Things (IoT) architecture, multimodal interaction, intelligent decision-making, edge computing, and data security. The review shows that AI technology has effectively improved the perception, interaction, and decision-making capabilities of smart home systems. Among these technologies, large language models (LLMs) enhance natural language understanding and user interaction capabilities, edge computing improves the real-time response efficiency of the system, and technologies such as blockchain provide new solutions for data security. At the same time, smart homes still face challenges in privacy protection, model reliability, cross-device collaboration, and standardization. In the future, modern smart home systems should be further integrated with artificial intelligence technologies, change traditional basic interaction modes, and promote the development of smart homes toward greater intelligence, security, and adaptability.
