documents.abstract: Teams of cooperative unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) are becoming crucial in scenarios where their complementary mobility, sensing capabilities, endurance, and physical interaction are beneficial. While UAVs offer fast aerial inspection and flexible perspectives, UGVs ensure large payloads, extended operation time, and the ability to intervene from ground level. Nonetheless, reliable UAV–UGV cooperation is challenging due to different dynamics, occasional communication, limited computational power, uncertain environments, and severe constraints on energy. This updated mini-review aims to bring together state-of-the-art and peer-reviewed research on using artificial intelligence (AI) for enhancing adaptive controllers in air-ground cooperation problems. This paper addresses four interconnected topics: learning-enabled control, model predictive and hybrid AI-model predictive control controllers, resilient coordination considering limited communication, and energy-conscious mission planning. As opposed to UAV–UGV surveys, this paper highlights the control-related aspects of air-ground cooperation, which include learning policies, constraint satisfaction, task allocation, degraded communication-based re-planning, and energy-dependent rendezvous. The revision significantly improves the process of selecting relevant literature, eliminates claims on benchmarks without evidence, updates unverified citations or references unrelated to the work, and produces publication-quality graphics. Ultimately, the review suggests that robust implementation would require explainable AI, rigorous sim-to-real transfer techniques, standardization of heterogeneous benchmarks, and efficient lightweight algorithms suitable for limited resources.
topics: Control and Dynamics of Mobile Robots

documents.abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a genetically and phenotypically heterogeneous myocardial disease associated with a broad spectrum of clinical outcomes, including heart failure, atrial fibrillation, ventricular arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) plays a central role in the comprehensive assessment of HCM by enabling integrated evaluation of myocardial morphology, ventricular and atrial function, tissue characterization, myocardial deformation, and longitudinal disease progression within a single comprehensive imaging modality. However, conventional CMR interpretation remains limited by manual post-processing, interobserver variability, sequence-dependent measurements, and reliance on a relatively restricted set of predefined imaging parameters. These limitations may hinder the full exploitation of the rich multidimensional information contained in CMR datasets. Artificial intelligence (AI) approaches, particularly machine learning and deep learning, together with radiomics-based quantitative image analysis, provide new opportunities to extend the diagnostic and prognostic value of CMR to extract high-dimensional and quantitative information from cine imaging, late gadolinium enhancement, parametric mapping, and feature-tracking-based deformation analysis. Emerging evidence suggests that AI-enhanced CMR may facilitate automated image analysis, improve diagnostic classification, support differentiation of HCM from phenocopies, enable tissue- and deformation-based phenotypic characterization, and enhance individualized risk prediction. Although several studies have included independent or external testing, many remain retrospective, rely on selected populations or internal validation, and lack prospective assessment of clinical utility. High discrimination performance should not be interpreted as established clinical utility, because calibration, decision-curve analysis, clinically relevant thresholds, and prospective clinical impact remain insufficiently evaluated. In addition, interpretability and clinical generalizability remain important challenges for translation into routine practice. This review summarizes the current role of CMR in HCM and discusses emerging applications, methodological challenges, and future directions of AI-enhanced CMR for diagnosis, phenotypic characterization, and risk stratification.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The incorporation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the design and analysis of renewable energy systems has become a revolutionary method for enhancing efficiency, reliability and sustainability. AI-driven models provide intelligent forecasting, optimization, and regulation of renewable energy sources, including solar, wind, hydro and biofuels. Utilizing techniques such as machine learning, deep learning, and evolutionary algorithms, AI enables precise forecasting of energy production, dynamic load regulation and fault identification. This chapter examines the approaches and frameworks for integrating AI into the design and performance evaluation of renewable energy systems. Focus is directed towards data-driven enhancement of system components, energy storage administration, and smart grid incorporation. The results indicate that AI integration improves energy conversion efficiency and operational stability while facilitating the shift to cleaner, more adaptable energy systems.

Can artists deliberately design artworks to be remembered—or forgotten? Across three experiments, we tested whether visual-memory outcomes can be shaped through artistic design and how they are predicted by artists, laypeople, and artificial intelligence. We launched a nationwide art contest in which artists submitted works intended to be memorable or forgettable. Using recognition tasks with adults based in the United States (119 from Amazon Mechanical Turk, 892 from Prolific, and 62 visitors from a Chicago gallery), we found that artists achieved their intended memory outcomes. However, their success was asymmetric: Memorability was more readily increased than reduced. A neural network, ResMem, consistently outperformed human observers and artists in predicting which artworks would be remembered. Data-driven analyses identified psychologically interpretable features that explained nearly half the variance in memory and aligned with ResMem’s predictions, but not with human judgments. Together, findings suggest that visual memorability can be engineered by humans, though asymmetrically, and is better captured by computational models.

With the proliferation of digital platforms and smartphones, users increasingly express opinions in their native languages through online reviews. However, fine-grained sentiment analysis for such low-resource languages remains underexplored, as most Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA) methods target resource-rich languages such as English. To address this gap, we present Odia-TriGCN, a hybrid framework for Aspect Sentiment Triplet Extraction in the low-resource Odia language. It integrates tree-distance relations (dependency and constituent trees), syntactic dependencies, and biaffine semantic attention to capture rich structural and semantic cues. The model further leverages auxiliary features from an Odia news corpus and cross-lingual supervision using an Odia–English parallel corpus. We also incorporate a customized dependency parser trained on manually annotated data following the Universal Dependencies (UD) scheme, to obtain consistent head-dependent relations. Additionally, we extend the existing Odia ABSA dataset and introduce Odia-Triplet , a manually annotated dataset comprising aspect-opinion-sentiment triplets. Experiments across five domains show that Odia-TriGCN outperforms the strongest compared non-LLM baseline in each domain by 5.6 to 7.1 absolute F1 points. The framework is further evaluated in cross-lingual (Odia → Hindi, Odia → Bengali) and code-mixed (Odia–English, Odia–Hindi–English, Odia–Bengali–English) settings, providing further evidence of its applicability in multilingual contexts.

BackgroundManual load-carrying remains common in developing countries and poses significant occupational health risks. However, integrated three-dimensional (frequency, severity, and interference)-based ergonomic assessment of the head porterage job is limited.ObjectiveThis study assesses the distribution of Musculoskeletal Discomfort (MSD) among head porters in selected open-air markets in Ibadan, Nigeria.MethodsA descriptive cross-sectional survey was done among 100 head-porters in Bodija, Oja-Oba, and Challenge markets using stratified and purposive sampling. Data were collected via an adapted Cornell Musculoskeletal Discomfort Questionnaire (CMDQ) and analysed by descriptive statistics. CMDQ scores for frequency, severity, and work interference were multiplied to obtain composite CMDQ index for each body region, while percentage CMDQ index (%CMDQ) was calculated to rank affected body regions. Data were analysed using chi-square tests and Spearman's rank correlation at a significance level of 0.05.ResultsMost participants were females (78.0%), aged 30-55 years (71.0%), and worked more than six hours per day (79.0%). MSD was widely reported across multiple body regions, with the lower back being the most affected, followed by the left thigh, right thigh, neck, and knees, with %CMDQ of 8.8, 7.8, 7.7, 7.6, and 7.2%, respectively. MSD frequently interfered with work performance and reduced job satisfaction. A weak, but statistically significant, positive correlation (r = 0.31, p < 0.05) was found between MSD severity and daily working hours.ConclusionsThe multidimensional approach provides a comparative empirical framework for prioritising MSD severity across body regions. The high ergonomic risk observed highlights urgent need for targeted interventions in the informal market environments.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: This study assessed the use of emerging technologies for digital preservation of indigenous knowledge among librarians in Bayelsa State libraries. The study was guided by two research questions that examined the emerging technologies available for digital preservation of indigenous knowledge and the extent to which librarians utilise these technologies in Bayelsa State libraries. The study adopted a descriptive survey research design. The population of the study comprised librarians working in selected academic and public libraries in Bayelsa State, Nigeria. An online survey questionnaire titled Use of Emerging Technologies for Digital Preservation of Indigenous Knowledge Questionnaire (UETDPIKQ) was used for data collection. A total of 127 responses were retrieved and used for the study. The data collected were analysed using frequency counts, percentages, mean, and standard deviation. The findings revealed that emerging technologies such as digitisation/scanning technologies, institutional repositories, cloud storage systems, digital archiving platforms, metadata applications, social media platforms, automated library systems, multimedia technologies, and internet/Wi Fi facilities were available in Bayelsa State libraries, with a grand mean score of 2.75 on a 4-point scale. However, artificial intelligence tools were found to be inadequately available. The study further revealed that librarians utilised emerging technologies for digital preservation of indigenous knowledge to a high extent, with a grand mean score of 3.43 on a 5-point scale. Technologies such as social media platforms, internet-based technologies, digitisation tools, institutional repositories, and cloud storage systems were widely used for indigenous knowledge preservation and dissemination. These findings suggest that, although foundational digital tools are gaining ground in Bayelsa State libraries, deliberate investment in artificial intelligence capacity is needed if librarians are to sustain and advance current preservation practice. The study concluded that although emerging technologies are increasingly available and utilised in Bayelsa State libraries, challenges relating to inadequate infrastructure, poor funding, and limited technological expertise continue to hinder effective digital preservation practices. The study recommended improved funding for digital preservation initiatives, provision of advanced technologies, continuous ICT training for librarians, improved internet connectivity, and stronger institutional support for sustainable indigenous knowledge preservation

Relevance. The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) assistants in professional settings introduces new forms of human–technology interaction. Perceiving an AI assistant as a human-like partner may be associated with users' confidence in their abilities and various aspects of occupational well-being. Objective. To examine the associations between perceived AI assistant anthropomorphism and employees' confidence in using AI, occupational self-efficacy, and two dimensions of occupational burnout: exhaustion and disengagement from work. Methods. Data from a cross-sectional online survey were analyzed. The initial dataset comprised 704 responses, of which 665 participants met the eligibility criteria for employment and regular AI use. After excluding four respondents who failed both attention checks, the final analytical sample consisted of 661 participants. The mean age was 30.06 years (SD = 7.34). Measures included the Godspeed, AISES, OSS, and OLBI scales. Descriptive statistics, internal consistency estimates, correlation analyses, and regression models were calculated. The interaction between perceived anthropomorphism and prior experience with AI was also examined. Results. The anthropomorphism measure (GOD_A) was positively correlated with the AI assistance and self-efficacy measure (AISES_AS; r = 0.148, 95% CI [0.073, 0.222], p < 0.001). Correlations with exhaustion (r = −0.010, p = 0.792) and disengagement (r = 0.024, p = 0.540) were not statistically significant. After controlling for AI use experience, age, and workload, the GOD_A coefficient in the AISES_AS regression model was β = 0.070 (p = 0.082). A statistically significant interaction between anthropomorphism and AI use experience was identified (b = 0.114, 95% CI [0.037, 0.191], p = 0.004). Conclusions. Perceived AI assistant anthropomorphism is associated with employees' confidence in using AI, with the nature of this association varying according to prior experience with the technology. No statistically significant direct association was identified between anthropomorphism and occupational burnout. These findings provide a foundation for further investigation into the psychological dimensions of AI implementation in organizational settings.

Background: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a global public health challenge, yet its relationship between occupational noise exposure and perceived noise impact remains unclear. Objective: We characterized maritime noise exposure patterns and examined the associations of noise exposure, perceived noise impact, and BMI with NAFLD among seafarers. Methods: A population-based survey was conducted from March to May 2024 through the China Shipowners' Association. Participants completed a structured online questionnaire. Noise exposure was assessed via self-report, and NAFLD presence was determined by self-reported physician diagnoses based on the 2018 updated NAFLD guidelines. Results: A total of 8143 male seafarers was included, with an overall NAFLD prevalence of 18.5% (n=1503). The prevalence was significantly higher among seafarers with a BMI of 24.0 kg/m² or above (25.9%, n=1261), chronic noise exposure (19.4%, n=1293), and higher perceived noise impact (slightly: 16.9%, n=589; moderate: 19.1%, n=359; significant: 22.5%, n=511). Among seafarers with a BMI of 24.0 kg/m² or above, chronic noise exposure and higher perceived noise impact were significantly associated with an elevated risk of NAFLD. After full adjustment, the combined association of chronic noise exposure and higher perceived noise impact remained significantly associated with increased NAFLD risk, with consistent patterns observed across both workplace and rest area settings. A significant interaction was also observed between rest-area noise exposure and perceived noise impact in this BMI subgroup. Conclusions: Noise exposure, perceived noise impact, and BMI were significantly associated with NAFLD among seafarers. These findings highlight the importance of optimizing occupational health benefits, especially among those with metabolic disorders.

Training recipes are tuned by hand for one model, cluster and workload, and every new model, accelerator, framework version or dataset means tuning again. Automated tuners search a fixed space of knobs and check only that a job runs, yet a configuration can run to completion while it silently changes training. ATTUNE is a single coding agent that tunes any working recipe for the workload and stack at hand, unattended, within a GPU-hour budget the user sets. It diagnoses each run and changes one lever at a time, guided by a catalog of lessons from past campaigns, and ships a recipe only if it passes a correctness gate: a configuration check against objective-changing settings and known stack defects, and a convergence check of its loss curve against the baseline's. On four held-out models at 64-128 GPUs, ATTUNE raises mean throughput over the strongest public recipe run on our stack by 6.7% on Llama-3.1-405B (best campaign 11.9%) and 33.9% on GLM-4.5 (54.7%), whose public recipe was written for H100. It keeps Mixtral-8x22B's recipe, where nothing it finds clears the noise band. Under a common GPU-hour budget it beats OptiCo, Bayesian optimization and random search on GLM-4.5 and MiniMax-M2; on GLM-4.5 its mean gain is more than four times the best alternative's at less than half the GPU-hours, and on both models its tuning pays for itself within a day of training. The gate rejects no legitimate run and catches 16 of 24 faulty runs, missing only ones that barely move the 20-step loss. Ablations tie its best campaigns to one of its search rules: retrying an out-of-memory layout with recomputation. We release ATTUNE's code and TrainingThroughputBench, a leaderboard of the fastest known recipes for MoE models up to 744B parameters on up to 256 GPUs, each with its throughput, cost per million tokens and a passed correctness check, at https://github.com/amazon-science/attune.

OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to validate a segmentation pipeline for the extraction of volumetric thigh muscle data, investigate the influence of demographics on segmentation performance, and investigate the influence of low-quality segmentations on quantitative performance and downstream metrics. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Manual thigh muscle segmentations on axial T1-weighted spin echo thigh images of 364 (106 training and validation; 258 testing) participants of the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) were used. A trained YOLO (You Only Look Once) object detection model generated labels and box predictions, that were passed to a fine-tuned foundation model (Segment Anything, Meta), which generated muscle segmentations. The quality of segmentations was assessed by two radiologists (none, minor, major issue), and Dice scores and mean bias versus manual segmentations were calculated in the testing dataset. Linear regression was used to calculate the associations of age, sex, and BMI with Dice scores. RESULTS: Dice scores ranged between 0.97 (quadriceps) and 0.89 (adductors). Exclusion of erroneous segmentations decreased mean bias by 0.06 mL across muscle groups; mean Dice of segmentations with versus without major issues was 0.90 versus 0.94. Female sex was associated with marginally lower Dice scores (beta -0.01, 95% CI: -0.02, -0.01, p < 0.001), while no other demographic feature showed significant associations. CONCLUSION: Foundation models can be fine-tuned on a modest task-specific dataset to achieve segmentation accuracy comparable to bespoke networks, without training a dedicated architecture from scratch. Visually erroneous segmentations introduce only negligible degradation of quantitative performance and downstream metrics and may thus be challenging to identify by data-driven detection strategies. KEY POINTS: Question Foundation models can be efficiently leveraged for robust segmentation on complex thigh muscle anatomy Findings Radiologist-identified erroneous segmentations introduced only negligible degradation of summary quantitative performance and are thus difficult to identify using statistical methods. Relevance statement Human-in-the-loop quality assurance post-validation adds limited value to improve downstream volumetric muscle metrics in foundation-model-based thigh segmentation. These findings carry implications for both research and potential clinical applications of muscle volume quantification, e.g., personalized therapeutic regimens.

Abstract—Contemporary enterprise Security Operations Centers (SOCs) are on the brink of systemic collapse driven by three converging factors: exponential alert fatigue (>25,000 uninvestigated alerts daily per enterprise), acute global cybersecurity workforce shortages, and the emergence of automated, machine-speed cyber threats executing multi-stage Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) in sub-minute time horizons. Traditional Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) platforms rely on brittle, rigid, hard-coded linear playbooks that fail when adversaries deviate slightly from known MITRE ATT&CK patterns. The paradigm of the Autonomous AI-Driven SOC (Autonomous SOC) establishes a transformative architecture that replaces rigid rule engines with specialized collaborative Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) powered by fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). In an Autonomous SOC, decentralized cognitive agents autonomously triage alerts, execute deep forensic graph correlation, synthesize non-linear incident playbooks, isolate compromised endpoints via zero-trust API invocations, and conduct automated counter-adversarial negotiations. However, deploying autonomous agentic execution in mission-critical defensive infrastructure exposes severe risks: catastrophic hallucination loops during remediation, prompt injection propagation across defensive pipelines, decision deadlock, and unauthorized disruption of legitimate enterprise operations. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of Autonomous SOC architectures. We formalize incident response as a decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) under dynamic threat uncertainty, model consensus verification over cryptographic remediation DAGs, and establish a dual-tier human-on-the-loop (HOTL) safety gating mechanism. Furthermore, we construct an enterprise SOC evaluation testbed spanning 10,000 multi-stage attack scenarios across real-world enterprise topologies. Our empirical findings demonstrate that our multi-agent autonomous framework slashes Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) from 18.4 minutes to 4.2 seconds and Mean Time to Remediate (MTTR) from 42.6 minutes to 18.2 seconds (a 99.3% reduction) while preserving a 99.6% remediation accuracy against MITRE ATT&CK kill chains. Finally, we formulate open challenges in adversarial prompt-injection resilience, continuous defensive co-evolution, and liability attribution under international cyber law. Index Terms—Autonomous SOC, Security Operations Center, Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), SOAR, Incident Response, MITRE ATT&CK, Dec-POMDP, Defensive AI, Alert Fatigue, Cyber Threat Intelligence.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: AI agents for autonomous scientific discovery must decide which experiments to run under a limited budget. Most benchmarks for science agents provide fixed datasets, while others that support active experimentation largely rely on simulation. We introduce Autonomous Science Bench, an initial release comprising six budgeted design-build-test-learn campaigns grounded in published experiments across biology, chemistry, and materials science. Agents select batches of designs, receive measurements from a lab service, and use the results to guide subsequent experiments before delivering a predictive model. Success requires passing two calibrated gates: a discovery gate, which evaluates the designs the agent measured, and a learning gate, which evaluates its model's ranking of held-out designs. In a pilot evaluation of eight agent-model configurations and 144 trials, the best configuration succeeds in 67% of trials, while the hardest campaign is solved in only three of 24 attempts. The two gates reveal different weaknesses: some agents build accurate rankings but find too few promising designs, while others find promising designs but fail to predict which unseen designs will perform well. These differences are obscured by overall success rates alone. We release version 0.1 of the campaigns, lab runtime, and public leaderboard at https://yibow.me/autonomous-science-bench.

Pre-trained Large Language Model (LLMs) are effective on many tasks in zero-shot and few-shot settings. For machine translation of low-resource languages, the obvious options are few-shot prompting and fine-tuning on a small parallel set. We ask: what if moderate amounts of low-resource monolingual data are also available? We argue that, rather than continued pretraining, a more effective use of this data is the pre-LLM era technique of back-translation (BT). The current fine-tuned LLM translates monolingual sentences in each language, and the resulting pairs train it in the reverse direction. Updates on the parallel set are interleaved for stable learning. With 1K parallel pairs on Odia and Swahili, BT beats continued pretraining into the low-resource language by 7.7 to 16.4 XCOMET-XXL points in domain. With beam-decoded intermediate translations, it also beats a model with 10 time more parallel data. In-context examples retrieved from the parallel data further improve BT. We also analyze the source, quality and amount of monolingual text. Across five low-resource languages, with Hindi as a high-resource control, and two 3B backbones, BT improves translation into the low-resource language by 16 to 173% XCOMET-XXL over parallel-only fine-tuning. Blind human evaluation on Odia and Sanskrit agrees with the automatic metrics.

Unintentional falls among older adults represent a severe global health concern, necessitating reliable, automated wearable Fall Detection Systems (FDS). However, developing practical wearable solutions requires navigating intricate engineering trade-offs among diagnostic accuracy, power consumption, memory footprint, and software development overhead. This paper presents a structured hardware selection guide evaluating three representative embedded design paradigms: low-cost threshold logic on 8-bit microcontrollers (Profile A), balanced classical machine learning on standard 32-bit platforms (Profile B), and compressed on-chip TinyML neural networks on edge-capable microcontrollers (Profile C). Comparative analysis reveals that while threshold methods achieve multi-week battery longevity at sub-$12 costs, they suffer from high false-alarm rates during dynamic daily activities. Conversely, TinyML architectures deliver superior classification accuracy (98%) on raw kinematic streams, but introduce steep memory quantization barriers, complex toolchains, and shorter battery recharge intervals. Classical machine learning emerges as the optimal design compromise for most developers, achieving robust diagnostic discrimination (95% sensitivity and specificity) with manageable computational demands at $15-$25. Finally, this review evaluates sensor placement ergonomics, addresses pervasive demographic bias in youth-simulated training datasets, and delivers a practical hardware selection framework for student researchers and independent developers.
topics: Wireless Sensor Networks for Data Analysis

documents.abstract: **Basic Principles and Practical Paths of LLM-Empowered Senior High School English Writing Evaluation in China: A Conceptual Framework** **Jiang Li** College of Education, Zhejiang Normal University, Jinhua 321004, China Zhengzhou No. 36 Middle School, Zhengzhou 450042, China **Abstract:** This paper adopts a conceptual analysis approach based on policy document interpretation and narrative literature synthesis to explore large language model empowered senior high school English writing evaluation within the Chinese educational context. Driven by national digital transformation of education and the 2020 Overall Plan for Deepening the Reform of Educational Evaluation in the New Era, generative large language models deliver innovative technical support to resolve prominent drawbacks of traditional writing assessment including superficial evaluation dimensions, single evaluation subjects, rigid marking mechanisms and delayed interactive feedback. Different from conventional automated writing evaluation tools limited to surface linguistic scoring, large language models generate conversational feedback, support adjustable evaluation standards through prompt design and conduct comprehensive discourse assessment covering language competence, cultural awareness, thinking quality and learning ability which forms the core innovation of this research. This study systematically elaborates two guiding orientations for human machine collaborative evaluation including disciplinary core literacy orientation and digital intelligent diversified evaluation orientation and constructs three targeted practical paths matching real senior high school teaching scenarios. The three paths cover teacher led evaluation guided by curriculum standards, visualized learner profiling for targeted instruction and cross time and space personalized writing guidance. Supplementary supporting measures regarding academic integrity, minor data compliance, balanced digital resource allocation and teacher artificial intelligence literacy cultivation are further supplemented to improve practical operability. The established framework helps shift assessment logic from score oriented judgment to literacy oriented developmental guidance. Restrictions such as algorithm bias, student over dependence on artificial intelligence and data ethical risks hinder stable large scale application of model based evaluation and relevant discussions are fully presented in the limitations section. This research provides theoretical frameworks and operable classroom strategies for intelligent reform of senior high school English writing evaluation in China. **Keywords:** Large Language Models; Automated Writing Evaluation; Formative Assessment; Senior High School EFL Writing; Disciplinary Core Literacy **Ctation:** Jiang, L. (2026). Basic Principles and Practical Paths of LLM-Empowered Senior High School English Writing Evaluation in China: A Conceptual Framework. _Social Sciences and Humanities Inquiry_, _1_(2), 55–65. https://doi.org/10.67728/sshi.2026.010

Long-context inference makes the key-value (KV) cache a major memory bottleneck for large language models. We propose BELT, a low-rank KV cache compression framework. Its key-side objective targets attention distributions rather than raw keys or pre-softmax logits, yielding a quadratic surrogate with a closed-form low-rank solution. A learned global rank allocator uses differentiable soft selection during training and hard selection at deployment to meet a user-specified component budget. Experiments demonstrate improved model quality under aggressive compression and increased decoding throughput at comparable accuracy. Evaluated across three LLMs and multiple benchmarks, BELT achieves up to 70% low-rank KV cache compression while outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 23.3 points on LongBench, and up to 17.8x overall KV cache reduction when combined with quantization. With Triton-based GPU kernels and a quantized cache, BELT delivers up to 2.7x speedup for the attention module and 3.3x end-to-end decoding throughput.

Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong zero-shot reasoning across diverse domains, but their potential for Human-Object Interaction (HOI) remains unexplored. Unlike traditional HOI approaches that rely on extensive labeled datasets and fixed interaction taxonomies, MLLMs offer flexible reasoning, making them well-suited for dynamic, real-world scenarios. In this work, we present the first systematic study of MLLMs for HOI recognition and detection within a pipeline that combines an external object detector for entity localization with zero-shot multimodal reasoning for interaction understanding. We introduce a benchmark framework for principled zero-shot evaluation, consisting of (i) a unified taxonomy of zero-shot prompting strategies, and (ii) a methodology that transforms token-level logits into interaction scores, enabling fair comparison with specialized HOI models under standard metrics. To support prompt-based evaluation, we additionally construct new question-answer annotations for standard HOI datasets, transforming them into a format suitable for MLLMs. Building on this, we propose two visual prompting strategies, namely Objects as Context and Black Other Objects, that guide MLLMs to target objects while preserving scene context. Experiments on HICO, HICO-DET, and V-COCO demonstrate state-of-the-art zero-shot performance, achieving 53.50 mAP on HICO and 23.69 mAP on HICO-DET. Overall, our work provides a principled benchmarking framework for MLLMs in HOI, opening the door to new models and datasets and enabling flexible open-world interaction understanding.

Purpose This paper proposes a pedagogical framework for cultivating inquiry-driven agency in student engagement with artificial intelligence (AI). It addresses a gap in the AI-in-education literature, in which substantial scholarly attention to material access and algorithmic fairness has been accompanied by comparatively less sustained attention to the learner-side capacities that determine whether AI is engaged with critically or passively. The paper offers three connected contributions: a cyclical model of inquiry-driven learning, a four-phase curricular sequence for student-AI engagement, and an operational assessment counterpart that remains diagnostically meaningful in AI-mediated environments. Design/methodology/approach The paper employs an integrative conceptual approach in the tradition of model-paper scholarship (Jaakkola, 2020). It synthesises five bodies of literature: AI in education and AI literacy frameworks, critical scholarship on educational technology, foundational work on curiosity, dual-process cognition, and adaptive expertise, constructive-developmental theory, and research on question-asking in learning and authentic assessment. Sources were identified through targeted citation tracing supplemented by database searches. Theoretical resources are justified at the point of use rather than methodologically up front. Findings The analysis demonstrates that material access and algorithmic fairness, while necessary, do not on their own account for the learner-side capacities that determine whether AI is engaged with critically or passively. It argues that inquiry-driven agency, the capacity to ask productive questions of AI rather than receive its answers, is a worthwhile object of pedagogical design. The Student-AI Learning Trajectory Model presents this development as a four-phase curricular sequence (AI as Tool, Machine, Object, and Partner), with progression understood as a curricular design decision made by educators rather than a developmental trigger inside the learner. Research limitations/implications The model is conceptual rather than empirically validated, and its applicability to younger learners, neurodiverse learners, and low-literacy contexts has not been fully worked out. The paper signposts several lines of empirical inquiry: longitudinal studies of SALT-informed curricula, methodological development of inquiry-sequence assessment instruments drawing on the Objective Structured Clinical Examination tradition, and comparative studies across institutional contexts and learner populations. The contribution is bounded to the pedagogical dimension and does not address the structural reforms that critical scholarship has identified as necessary for genuine educational equity. Practical implications The paper has implications for curriculum design, educator development, and assessment practice. Curricula can sequence student-AI engagement across phases of increasing sophistication rather than treating AI literacy as content to be covered. Educator development requires sustained investment in pedagogical capacity, particularly the modelling of inquiry-driven engagement in front of students. Institutions should treat the redesign of assessment for the AI era as a pedagogical question rather than an integrity question, with inquiry-sequence assessment offering one operational direction. Equity-oriented investment should prioritise educator capacity over the mass distribution of adaptive learning software. Social implications The cultivation of inquiry capacity in AI-mediated learning environments matters for the kinds of learners that schools and universities send into a world increasingly shaped by automated systems. Without deliberate pedagogical design, AI risks becoming a multiplier of existing educational divides rather than a neutralising force. The model locates responsibility with institutions and educators designing learning environments, not with individual students, and identifies the risk of a pedagogical Matthew Effect in which inquiry-driven pedagogy becomes available primarily to already advantaged students absent institutional investment in educator capacity. Originality/value The paper brings together three conversations that have developed largely in parallel: AI literacy as a set of competencies, evaluative judgement as a response to generative AI's destabilisation of assessment, and curiosity as a driver of self-directed learning. Its distinctive contribution is the articulation of phase progression as a curricular sequence informed by a cyclical model of inquiry learning, complemented by an operational assessment counterpart. The paper offers vocabulary and tools for educators, curriculum designers, and assessment scholars responding to the question of how AI should be integrated into the work of cultivating independent learners.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Universities are rapidly adopting artificial intelligence, yet access to AI tools does not guarantee that students experience greater ownership of their learning. This study examines how three learner side factors, AI literacy, AI readiness and perceived value of AI tools, and one pedagogy side factor, AI enhanced instructional design, relate to perceived autonomous learning outcomes. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model and Self Determination Theory, we conducted a cross sectional online survey of students in Indian higher education who had used AI supported tools for academic purposes in the previous six months. After data cleaning, 516 valid responses were analysed. The measurement model showed strong reliability and convergent validity, and discriminant validity was supported (all HTMT values below 0.85). A simultaneous multiple regression explained 46.7 percent of the variance in perceived autonomous learning outcomes (F(4, 511) = 111.887, p < .001). All four factors were positively associated with the outcome, with AI literacy the strongest (β = .336), followed by AI enhanced instructional design (β = .178), perceived value of AI tools (β = .147) and AI readiness (β = .120). Because the data are self reported, cross sectional and drawn from a nonprobability sample, the results indicate associations among perceptions, not causal effects or objective learning gains. The findings suggest that institutions should pair AI adoption with systematic AI literacy development and thoughtful instructional design, treating student agency rather than tool availability as the goal.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Theory of mind (ToM), the ability to reason about others' mental states, underlies effective communication and coordination. Its higher-order form enables reasoning over nested perspectives in strategic interactions. However, existing evaluations often equate belief-nesting depth with reasoning order, allowing nominally higher-order questions to admit lower-order shortcuts. We formalize effective order through the distinct events supporting successive belief prefixes, revealing widespread order inflation across existing benchmarks. We introduce HopToM, with certified full-order questions and controls for lower-order alternatives. Under direct prompting, mean accuracy across four frontier LLMs falls from 73.5% at first order to 20.0% at fourth order, and human participants also struggle. Causal interventions link a recurring class of errors to evidence for shallower belief prefixes. We introduce HopTrace, a plug-and-play inference-time method that encodes each interaction once into perspective records and resolves nested queries deterministically. On certified narrative questions, it improves fourth- and fifth-order accuracy by 22.0 and 38.5 percentage points over strong prompting baselines, while using 20-39 times fewer tokens than multi-call methods. These results sharpen how higher-order ToM is evaluated and offer a practical way to improve perspective reasoning in interactive agents.

This preregistration describes a scoping review examining the sociotechnical implications of AI-augmented gamification in higher education. The review will map how artificial intelligence techniques are integrated with gamification mechanisms and analyze their relationship with learner autonomy, learner agency, digital inequality, privacy, surveillance, datafication, algorithmic bias, transparency, algorithmic governance, and human control. The review will follow JBI methodology for scoping reviews, report according to PRISMA-ScR, and document database searches in accordance with PRISMA-S. Eligible studies will include peer-reviewed journal articles and conference proceedings published in English or Spanish between 2011 and the final search date in 2026. Searches will be conducted in Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, and ACM Digital Library, complemented by backward and forward citation searching. The objective is to provide an integrated sociotechnical synthesis of how AI-augmented gamification shapes learning, institutional decision-making, learner agency, and equity in higher education.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Nine deployed conversational systems mostly recognised the crisis, but it disappeared from their behaviour once the conversation moved on. We ran 16 scenarios in ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini as 14-message conversations (48 dialogues): crisis signals alternated with distraction, turn 13 introduced a new person at risk, and turn 14 was sent a day later. Coding was binary, as in the previous study, with clinical verification; two crisis-contour specifications were tested separately. New crisis signals drew a reaction in 87, 95, and 76 of 96 responses, respectively; the crisis stopped being mentioned mainly at an everyday message. The new person at risk drew a reaction in 44 of 48 responses; after a day, 29 retained crisis content. All 14 turns drew a 'yes' code in 4, 7, and 0 of 16 conversations. Reacting to the new person did not guarantee correct allocation of roles and actions. Both contour specifications produced safety-relevant errors. Neither hypothesis was supported: the systems behaved differently, and the same rule, introduced as a single package, did not stabilise their behaviour. Recognition, retention, and reconfiguration at a transition are distinct properties; the weakest is retention of the prior state and tracking of each person's trajectory.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is expanding AI-mediated informal digital learning of English (AI-IDLE) from predominantly receptive and conversational activities to cognitively demanding productive tasks such as academic writing. Yet little is known about how learners’ motivation and technology-related emotions develop over time, or how sustained interaction with GenAI may engage human capacities for evaluation and adaptation. Grounded in Complex Dynamic Systems Theory (CDST), this study investigated the longitudinal development of willingness to write (WTW), technology-related enjoyment (ENY), and technology-related anxiety (ANX) among Chinese undergraduates learning English as a Foreign Language (EFL) in teacher-supported AI-IDLE embedded within an 11-week English for Academic Purposes writing course. Twenty-six participants with complete records across 11 measurement occasions were included in the longitudinal analysis. Trajectory analysis, change-point analysis, and exploratory moving-window correlation analysis were combined with thematic analysis of learners’ reflections. WTW followed a nonlinear trajectory, declining during the middle period before a potential late-stage transition and subsequent increase, whereas ENY remained comparatively stable and ANX generally declined. The relationships of WTW with ENY and ANX also varied over time. Learners’ reflections revealed increasing recognition of human–AI complementarity and more selective, critical, and strategic engagement with GenAI. From a human-intelligence perspective, these patterns illustrate adaptive and metacognitive capacities involved in evaluating AI-generated information, adjusting strategies, and coordinating human and artificial resources. Rather than treating WTW or emotions as measures of intelligence, the findings position AI-IDLE as a context in which such human intellectual capacities may be exercised and expressed.

Small fiber neuropathy (SFN) is a sensory–autonomic neuropathy of thinly myelinated Aδ and unmyelinated C fibers that can produce neuropathic pain and multisystem autonomic symptoms. Although diagnostic criteria and confirmatory testing have improved recognition, SFN burden may remain underrecognized even after diagnosis. This narrative review identifies two complementary documentation failures. The translation problem arises when symptom labels and intensity ratings do not capture effects on sustainable function, cognitive workload, emotional well-being, and participation. The fragmentation problem arises when specialties assess multisystem symptoms without preserving their temporal pattern, co-occurrence, shared triggers, treatment trade-offs, and recovery costs. Reverse availability bias is proposed as a conceptual mechanism that may intensify both failures: symptoms or mechanisms not represented in clinicians’ mental models may be overlooked in consideration and documentation. The review proposes an SFN Burden Integration Framework (SFN-BIF) that separates symptom presence, burden, and causal attribution and combines validated measures with six core documentation fields: temporal pattern, triggers and relievers, co-occurrence, recovery cost, functional consequences, and cognitive–emotional consequences. Longitudinal patient-reported information is integrated with neurological examination, skin biopsy, quantitative sensory testing, autonomic or organ-specific testing, and cognitive or functional assessment when indicated. Better integration may inform diagnosis and referral, treatment selection and trade-offs, rehabilitation and psychological care, disability assessment, phenotyping, and clinical trial outcome selection while preserving diagnostic rigor. The framework remains conceptual and requires prospective evaluation of validity, feasibility, clinical utility, and administrative burden. Small fiber neuropathy affects small sensory and autonomic nerves that help the body feel pain, temperature, and itch and regulate automatic functions such as sweating, digestion, heart rate, bladder function, and body temperature. Although recognized symptoms and diagnostic tests exist, the full burden of the condition may still be missed. Symptoms are often recorded as labels or scores without showing what they prevent, interrupt, or force a person to manage. Different specialists may also assess symptoms across body systems, so timing, shared triggers, interactions, treatment trade-offs, and recovery costs can be lost. This review proposes a patient-informed approach that keeps three questions separate: Is a symptom present? What burden does it cause? How certain is its connection to small fiber neuropathy? The approach combines standard questionnaires and clinical measures with brief documentation of when symptoms occur, what triggers or relieves them, which symptoms occur together, how long recovery takes, and how they affect daily activities, mental effort, and emotional well-being. Patient reports do not replace neurological examination, skin biopsy, sensory or autonomic testing, or other clinically indicated assessments. Instead, they add longitudinal and functional information that isolated tests and appointments may not capture. Better integration may support treatment choices, rehabilitation, communication between specialists, disability assessment, and research while preserving appropriate uncertainty about the cause of individual symptoms.

Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has expanded access to digital-solution creation by enabling users to develop applications through natural-language interaction. However, successful initiation does not always lead to reliable completion because users still encounter technical, contextual, and integration challenges that require further adaptation. This study aims to examine how community-mediated adaptation shapes GenAI-enabled digital work transformation, particularly when prompt-based solution development experiences breakdowns. A process-oriented netnographic approach was employed to analyze naturally occurring interactions within a private Indonesian WhatsApp community of OKEGAS users. The dataset consisted of 10,444 user-generated messages, which were screened to identify 177 relevant conversation episodes comprising 1,419 messages from 190 pseudonymized sender identifiers. The findings reveal a recurring process involving prompt-mediated solution initiation, breakdown, peer diagnosis, and adaptive work reconfiguration. User responses after breakdown occurred through recovery-oriented and redirection-oriented adaptation, including repair attempts, rollback, tool or model switching, infrastructure changes, simplification, and discontinuance. These trajectories resulted in varied outcomes, ranging from reported stabilization and deployment progress to persistent failure or abandonment. The study contributes to Technology Affordance Theory by introducing community-mediated adaptation as a post-breakdown pathway in which peer involvement expands the user-AI relationship into a user-AI-peer configuration. The findings highlight that GenAI accessibility must be complemented by human judgment, peer knowledge, and technical capabilities to achieve dependable digital work transformation.

Purpose – Fear of missing out (FOMO) is increasingly invoked to explain corporate rushes toward emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), yet it has neither been distinguished from bandwagon and imitation explanations of adoption nor traced from the individual executive to the organizational decision. This study examines whose loss executives anticipate when they experience FOMO, how FOMO differs from bandwagon pressure, and through which pathways it becomes an organizational adoption decision.Design/methodology/approach – An inductive study of the adoption of AI-based voice assistants, such as Amazon Alexa, by global consumer packaged goods firms, drawing on 63 in-depth interviews (42 executives from 19 firms and 21 voice-technology suppliers) and 115 archival documents. Explicit coding rules separate FOMO from bandwagon pressure and imitation heuristics.Findings – FOMO is an anticipatory affective state rather than a decision rule. It manifests with three referents, namely the executive (employee), the team and the firm, which differ in target, relevance and response. Firm-referent FOMO produces convergence with peers, whereas employee- and team-referent FOMO produce divergence, a rush to be first. FOMO can arise before any peer has adopted and reaches the organizational decision through four pathways (downward cascade, upward issue selling, lateral rivalry and external amplification), typically resulting in a bounded test-and-learn commitment.Originality/value – The study positions FOMO as the affective micro-foundation of bandwagon behavior, provides a referent-based typology, and identifies how individual FOMO aggregates into organizational decisions, with practical guidance for bounding FOMO-driven initiatives.

Test-time scaling for large language models (LLMs) can involve generating multiple candidate solutions for selection or revising an earlier attempt. To guide selection and revision, we need a verifier that can estimate candidate correctness and provide evidence of failure. In competitive programming, however, official judging systems provide authoritative verdicts under finite submission budgets, without revealing failure explanations or failing inputs. To provide informative feedback without consuming official submissions, we formulate a task in which a model judges and diagnoses a candidate program using only the problem statement and source code, with generated counterexamples serving as checkable evidence. To evaluate this task, we build USACO-JUDGE from the USACO 2026 contests, using accepted and unaccepted programs written by human experts and multiple LLMs. We then train ARBITER, a 35B mixture-of-experts (MoE) agentic verifier, with reinforcement learning in a generic execution sandbox. Training raises counterexample success on incorrect programs from 40.61% to 62.67% and mean binary verdict accuracy on USACO-JUDGE from 71.41% to 87.41%, approaching frontier verification performance. Beyond verification, ARBITER outperforms baselines in both code selection and refinement. In an IOI 2026 case study, ARBITER-guided refinement raises GPT-OSS-120B's expected score above the gold-medal threshold under the official submission limit.

topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Electrotactile stimulation, as a haptic feedback method, often struggles to evoke high-quality natural sensations. Consequently, despite its practical advantages, it is generally less preferred in human-machine systems than mechanical approaches. In this paper, we propose a bio-inspired stimulation framework that generates signals modelled on afferent neural activity derived from a touch model. By producing more biologically plausible spiking patterns, the proposed approach aims to enhance the realism of perceived tactile sensations. To evaluate these stimulation patterns in a realistic task context and to quantify the influence of visual and movement cues, we conducted a series of subjective experiments under three conditions. The results indicate that bio-inspired modulation was effective: in particular, bio-inspired co-modulation of amplitude and frequency achieved a favourable pressure-irritation trade-off, increasing the probability of perceiving pressure while maintaining low irritation (pressure: 0.78; irritation: 0.24) relative to the other patterns. Visual cues and hand movement further improved feedback quality by significantly increasing the probability of reporting pressure (p$<$0.001) without a corresponding increase in irritation, and by increasing mean naturalness ratings. Overall, these findings demonstrate the potential of bio-inspired electrotactile patterns to improve haptic feedback quality, and highlight the importance of evaluating such methods under realistic, multimodal interaction scenarios.

Abstract Deep learning has been widely adopted in the field of bioacoustics, enabling behavioral and ecological research into many sound producing animals through the use of specially designed and trained models. So-called foundational models can generalize to novel species or tasks, but require larger and more diverse training datasets. But the broad range of frequencies that animals produce poses a problem: bioacoustic datasets are recorded at various sample rates to capture different frequency ranges. Combining these data to train generalist models becomes exceedingly costly the wider the frequency range is expanded with high resolution data, becoming untenable for bioacousticians. To approach this problem, we performed experiments using a state-of-the-art transformer model, animal2vec, and a custom dataset consisting of recordings with various sample rates and species whose vocalizations cover a broad frequency range. We designed a positional encoding that provides inductive information about the sample rate, but found that the model is natively able to compensate for the perceived time stretch in the receptive field induced by varying sample rates, with no effect on performance compared to the standard approach of upsampling. This opens up new possibilities of training powerful models on broad bioacoustic datasets and the creation of more generalizable tools for bioacousticians.

This article examines the improvement of methodologies for developing primary school students’ logical thinking through digital didactic games. In contemporary education, the integration of digital technologies into the learning process and the development of students’ independent thinking, analytical abilities, and problem-solving skills have become important pedagogical priorities. In primary mathematics education, interactive and age-appropriate learning activities play a significant role in fostering logical reasoning and enhancing students’ cognitive engagement. The article analyzes the educational potential of digital didactic games, the methodological foundations of their application in mathematics lessons, and their contribution to the development of primary school students’ cognitive abilities. Particular attention is given to approaches that help students develop comparison, classification, generalization, pattern recognition, logical reasoning, and problem-solving skills. The article also discusses the selection of appropriate digital games, the organization of tasks according to their levels of difficulty, the consideration of individual learning needs, and the assessment of educational outcomes. The proposed methodological recommendations aim to improve the effectiveness of primary mathematics instruction, increase students’ interest in learning, and support the systematic development of logical thinking. The findings and recommendations presented in the article may serve as a practical resource for primary school teachers seeking to integrate digital educational resources into classroom instruction.

The diffusion of digital technologies has shifted brand marketing from mass communication toward individualized consumer dialogue, and personalization has become a central capability for competitive differentiation. This paper examines how global brands design and implement personalization strategies in digital marketing environments, using L'Oréal, the world's largest cosmetics group, as a case. Drawing on a qualitative, single-case design and secondary data, including corporate reports, press releases, and peer-reviewed research, the study analyzes L'Oréal's personalization initiatives across four dimensions: data infrastructure and artificial intelligence (AI)-based diagnostics, augmented reality (AR) virtual try-on services, omnichannel customer relationship management, and personalized content delivered through influencers and social platforms. The findings indicate that L'Oréal's approach rests on proprietary technology ownership, systematic integration of AI and AR into the consumer journey, and organizational structures that connect data science with brand management. The case also reveals tensions involving privacy, algorithmic bias, and digital exclusion that condition the effectiveness of personalization. The study contributes an integrated framework that links AI capabilities to personalization touchpoints and brand outcomes, and offers managerial guidance for consumer goods firms seeking to scale personalization without eroding consumer trust.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Solid electrolytes (SEs) are central to next-generation metal batteries, yet their discovery remains constrained by fragmented data, limited transferability of simulations, and slow experimental iteration. Unlike catalysis, where surface reactivity dominates, SEs require simultaneous optimization of bulk ion transport, defect chemistry, mechanical integrity, and interfacial stability. Here, we outline a framework for autonomous SE discovery enabled by large artificial intelligence (AI) models, including machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) and large language models (LLMs). We discuss the evolution from static materials databases to dynamic, self-updating knowledge systems, the role of MLIPs in bridging density functional theory (DFT) and long-timescale ion migration, and the emergence of LLMs as engines for literature mining, hypothesis generation, and scientific reasoning. We further describe a closed-loop architecture integrating AI-driven candidate design, multiscale simulation, uncertainty-aware selection, and experimental validation. Such systems shift SE research from intuition-guided exploration to data-informed, self-improving cycles. We conclude by highlighting challenges in data standardization, interfacial complexity, and reproducibility, and we propose design principles for building autonomous laboratories for solid-state battery materials.

In many countries, National Climate Scenarios or Projections have become foundational components of national climate services, providing authoritative, science-based, locally tailored information to support climate-sensitive planning and policy. Drawing on the experiences of ten countries, this paper synthesizes current practices and identifies shared challenges in developing scientifically credible and decision-relevant climate information. Despite substantial progress, gaps persist between what users request and what climate scientists can deliver, reflecting limits in observations, models, methods, capacity, and the inherent uncertainties of weather and future climate change. Developments in climate science, including advances in (global) convection-permitting modelling, artificial intelligence and machine learning-based methods, and new generations of CMIP/CORDEX, together with expanding societal expectations, create both opportunities and dilemmas for updating and maintaining scenario products at a national scale. We highlight five outstanding questions: how to co-develop useful and credible products with diverse users; how to represent and communicate uncertainty at the science–policy interface; how to combine multiple lines of evidence across models, scales, and methods; how to integrate information on extreme events and low-likelihood, high-impact climate outcomes; and where national approaches should converge or remain nation-specific. Addressing these questions requires progress in, and collaboration between, physical climate science, the emerging science of climate services, and the social sciences. By strengthening user engagement, refining approaches to uncertainty, and expanding international collaboration to reduce duplication and raise standards, future National Climate Scenario services can provide a stronger foundation for climate information, risk assessment, adaptation planning, and associated policy processes.

Web development is changing as businesses adopt new technologies to improve their digital services. Companies need websites, web applications, and software platforms that offer a smooth user experience, protect customer data, and support business growth. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is adding new capabilities to this process by helping developers write code, test applications, solve technical problems, and build intelligent features. Full-stack development gives professionals the skills to work on both the front end and the back end of an application. When combined with AI-powered development tools, these skills can help developers build useful digital products and adapt to changing industry requirements. For aspiring professionals, a career in web development involves more than learning a programming language. It requires an understanding of application design, databases, APIs, testing, deployment, and security. AI knowledge can extend these skills by helping developers automate routine tasks and integrate intelligent services into web applications. The Changing Role of Web Developers Web developers traditionally build and maintain websites and applications by writing code, connecting databases, testing features, and fixing errors. Modern development also requires collaboration with designers, product managers, security teams, and other engineers. AI tools are changing parts of this workflow. Developers can use them to generate code suggestions, explain unfamiliar functions, draft documentation, and create initial test cases. This may reduce time spent on some repetitive tasks. However, AI-generated code is not always correct or secure. Developers must understand the underlying logic and check the output before using it in a live application. They must also confirm that the code meets performance requirements and follows the project's standards. This change increases the value of problem-solving and technical judgement. Developers who understand programming fundamentals can evaluate AI suggestions more effectively than those who depend on generated code without understanding it. A career in web development can therefore benefit from a balanced skill set that combines coding knowledge, AI literacy, communication, and continuous learning. Research and Market Trends Shaping Career Opportunities Industry research provides useful evidence about the skills and technology roles expected to become more important. These trends support the case for learning full-stack development and AI, although they do not guarantee employment for individual candidates.Learners exploring a Gen-AI Powered Full Stack Developer Course in Ameerpet can use this growing intersection of software engineering and artificial intelligence as a starting point for developing industry-relevant skills. Global employment outlook The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 identifies software and application developers among the fastest-growing job categories through 2030. It also lists AI and big data, networks and cybersecurity, and technological literacy among the skills expected to increase in importance. The report draws on more than 1,000 employers representing over 14 million workers across 55 economies. Its findings indicate that technology-related changes will affect both job requirements and workforce training. For aspiring web developers, this highlights the importance of learning core programming skills while remaining open to new tools and development methods. India's technology industry NASSCOM's Annual Strategic Review 2025 estimated that India's technology industry generated more than US$282.6 billion in revenue in FY2025, including hardware. It also projected that the industry could reach US$300 billion in FY2026. Engineering research and development, digital engineering, and global capability centres are among the areas contributing to India's technology ecosystem. These organisations support software development, product engineering, cloud services, and business transformation. This industry context creates a reason for learners to develop relevant technical skills. However, overall industry revenue is not the same as the number of available web development jobs. Actual hiring depends on employer requirements, business conditions, experience, and technical ability. Research on AI-assisted programming A controlled experiment published by researchers associated with Microsoft Research examined the effect of GitHub Copilot on a JavaScript programming task. Participants with access to the AI assistant completed the specified task 55.8% faster than participants in the control group. This result demonstrates the potential value of AI assistance in a defined setting. It does not mean that every software project will be completed at the same speed. Complex applications still require design, testing, security reviews, debugging, and coordination between team members. The practical lesson is to use AI tools to support development while retaining human responsibility for the final product. Core Skills for a Career in Full Stack Development A strong technical foundation helps developers build applications that work reliably. AI tools can support this process, but they cannot replace an understanding of how software systems operate. Front-end development Front-end development focuses on the interface users interact with. HTML provides structure, CSS controls presentation, and JavaScript adds interactive features. Developers can also learn frameworks such as React to create reusable components and manage complex interfaces. Responsive design and accessibility are important because applications must work across different devices and meet the needs of different users. AI assistants can help create initial interface components, but developers must check the design, usability, browser compatibility, and performance. Back-end development Back-end development handles application logic, data processing, authentication, and communication between services. Common technologies include Node.js, Python, Java, and their related frameworks. Developers should understand how to create APIs, manage user permissions, validate inputs, and handle errors. These skills help them build applications that are reliable and secure. Databases and APIs Databases store information such as customer profiles, orders, transactions, and product records. Knowledge of SQL, database design, data validation, and access control helps developers manage this information. APIs connect different systems. A web application may use them to communicate with payment gateways, cloud platforms, analytics services, or AI models. Understanding these connections is essential when building complete applications. Cloud, DevOps, and security Web development does not end when the code is written. Applications must be deployed, monitored, updated, and protected against security threats. Developers can benefit from learning Git, automated testing, continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD), containers, and cloud platforms. They should also understand secure authentication, data privacy, and the risks of exposing confidential information to unapproved AI tools. A Gen-AI Powered Full Stack Developer Course in Ameerpet can be considered by learners who want to study these technologies as part of a structured development path. Using AI Tools to Build Better Applications AI can support developers throughout the application lifecycle, from planning to maintenance. Its usefulness depends on the task, the quality of the input, and the developer's ability to evaluate the output. Code generation and debugging AI coding assistants can suggest functions, explain error messages, and create initial versions of repetitive code. Developers can use these suggestions to explore possible solutions and learn unfamiliar technologies. Before accepting generated code, they should review the logic, run tests, and check for security issues. This practice helps reduce the risk of introducing errors into an application. AI-powered application features Generative AI can help businesses add features such as chat assistants, document summaries, natural-language search, and personalised recommendations. For example, a customer support application could use an AI model to answer questions based on approved company documents. The full stack developer would build the user interface, manage access controls, connect APIs, and create the systems required to retrieve relevant information. Retrieval-augmented generation and AI agents Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) connects AI models with information retrieved from selected data sources. It can help applications produce responses based on relevant documents rather than relying only on information learned during model training. AI agents can use approved tools to complete defined multi-step tasks. These systems require clear permissions, monitoring, error handling, and human oversight when actions carry risk. Learning these concepts can help developers move beyond basic websites and explore more advanced applications. Career Paths and Professional Scope Full stack development can support several career paths, depending on a candidate's interests, technical knowledge, and experience. Full Stack Developer: Builds and maintains both front-end and back-end components. Front-End Developer: Creates interactive and accessible user interfaces. Back-End Developer: Develops server-side systems, APIs, and database connections. AI Application Developer: Integrates AI models and services into software products. Software Engineer: Designs, tests, and maintains software systems. Cloud or DevOps Engineer: Supports deployment, infrastructure, automation, and application monitoring. documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing where competitive advantage comes from in telecommunications. It used to depend mainly on network assets - spectrum, infrastructure, reach. Increasingly, it depends on how intelligent, adaptable, and resilient the systems running those assets are. This paper builds on the Comprehensive Techno-Economic (CTE) Model and its AI-augmented extension (AI-CTE) to propose a resilience framework that covers both autonomous network operations and autonomous business operations. Previous AI-CTE work formalized AI maturity, augmentation, dependency, and governance constructs, but mostly at the Technical Level. This paper extends that work in two directions. First, it introduces a Network Resilience Composite, combining the existing AI Resilience Score with a new Shock Absorption Capacity metric to quantify how well autonomous networks withstand and recover from disruptive events. Second, it develops three new AI-augmented equations at the Business Level - product and service resilience, customer and revenue resilience, and workforce resilience - which together make up a Business Resilience Index. These technical and business constructs, together with an Environmental/Governance Resilience Index, are combined into a single Telecom Operator Resilience Index (TORI). An illustrative application, extending a previously published case study, shows how the index can expose a gap between strong technical autonomy and weaker business-level resilience, giving operators concrete guidance on where to prioritize AI investment. The paper closes with an implementation roadmap and a discussion of limitations and future research directions. KeyWords: Comprehensive Techno-Economic Model, AI-CTE, Organizational Resilience, Autonomous Networks, Telecom Operators, AI Maturity Indeks.
